## Appendix E Incomplete Information Posted Price Mechanism

Here, we tackle the true Bayesian setting, when the posted price mechanism is not restricted to point-mass distributions. To do so, we first introduce some further notation from [DKL20]. Write $\mathbf{v}$ for the valuation vector coming from distribution $\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}_{1}\times\mathcal{D}_{2}\cdots\times\mathcal{D}_{n}.$ Respectively, write $\mathsf{OPT}(\mathbf{v})$ for (an) optimal allocation with valuations $\mathbf{v},$ where $\mathsf{OPT}(\mathbf{v})=(\mathsf{OPT}_{1}(\mathbf{v}),\mathsf{OPT}_{2}(\mathbf{v}),\ldots,\mathsf{OPT}_{n}(\mathbf{v})).$ Denote the social welfare under these valuations by $\mathbf{v}(\mathsf{OPT}(\mathbf{v})).$ Phrased in these terms, we need to design a posted price mechanism with expected social welfare $\Omega\left(\frac{\log\log q}{\log\log m}\right)\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{v}}[\mathbf{v}(\mathsf{OPT}(\mathbf{v}))].$

The set $\Delta$ is defined as in Section 4. We also need the following extra notation, which extends $\Delta$ to $n$ -tuples of distributions.

$$ \Gamma(p):=\left\{\{\nu^{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\in\Delta(p)|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{P}_{S\longleftarrow\nu^{i}}[j\in S]\leq p\text{ holds for all }j\in[m]\right\}. $$

Now, the equivalent statement to Lemma 4.0.2 in the framework of [DKL20] is the following.

#### Lemma E.0.1 ([DKL20, p.268]).

A class of monotone valuations $\mathcal{G}$ over $[m]$ and a product distribution $\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}_{1}\times\mathcal{D}_{2}\cdots\times\mathcal{D}_{n}$ over valuations in $\mathcal{G}$ are given. If there exists a real number $p\in[0,1]$ (possibly depending on $\mathcal{D}$ ), such that

$$ \mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{v}}\left[\sup_{\lambda\in\Gamma(p)}\inf_{\mu\in\Delta(p)}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}_{S_{i}\longleftarrow\lambda^{i},T_{i}\longleftarrow\mu}\mathbf{v}^{i}(S_{i}\backslash T_{i})\right]\geq\alpha\times\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{v}}[\mathbf{v}(\mathsf{OPT}(\mathbf{v}))], $$

then there exists an $\alpha$ -competitive posted price mechanism for the product distribution $\mathcal{D}.$

As in Section 4, we prove that when $\mathcal{G}$ is the set of $q$ -partitioning valuations, the above lemma holds with $\alpha=\Omega\left(\frac{\log\log q}{\log\log m}\right).$ The incomplete information case, however, is more technically challenging, so we break the proof into several lemmas. First, we need some more notation. Denote

$$ g^{\mathbf{v}}(q)=\sup_{\lambda\in\Gamma(p)}\inf_{\mu\in\Delta(p)}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}_{S_{i}\longleftarrow\lambda^{i},T_{i}\longleftarrow\mu}[\mathbf{v}^{i}(S_{i}\backslash T_{i})] $$

for any valuation vector $\mathbf{v}$ and

$$ f^{\mathbf{v}}(q)=\sup_{\lambda\in\Gamma(p)}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}_{S_{i}\longleftarrow\lambda^{i}}\mathbf{v}^{i}(S_{i}). $$

Again, we assume that $q>4$ is a perfect power of $2$ and $q=2^{r},s=\lceil\log_{\frac{r}{2}}\log_{16}m^{2}\rceil.$ Let $\displaystyle L=\left\{{-\left(\frac{r}{2}\right)^{i}}|i\in\{0,1,\ldots,s-1\}\right\}.$ Note that $|L|=s.$ Our first lemma is the following

#### Lemma E.0.2.

For any vector $\mathbf{v}$ of $q$ -partitioning valuations, the following inequality holds

$$ \frac{1}{s}\sum_{\ell\in L}g^{\mathbf{v}}(16^{\ell})\geq\frac{1}{8s}\left(\frac{1}{16}-\frac{1}{m}\right)\mathbf{v}(\mathsf{OPT}(\mathbf{v})). $$

#### Proof.

Note that $f^{\mathbf{v}}(16^{-1})\geq\frac{1}{16}\mathbf{v}(\mathsf{OPT}(\mathbf{v})).$ Indeed, the vector of independent distributions $(\lambda^{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ such that $S_{i}\longleftarrow\lambda^{i}$ satisfies $S_{i}=\mathsf{OPT}_{i}(\mathbf{v})$ with probability $1/16$ and $S_{i}=\emptyset$ with probability $15/16$ is in $\Gamma(16^{-1}).$ This is true because the sets $\mathsf{OPT}_{i}(\mathbf{v})$ are disjoint. Similarly, $f^{\mathbf{v}}(\frac{1}{m^{2}})\leq\frac{1}{m}$ holds as shown in [DKL20, Lemma A.2]. Therefore, using the telescoping trick in Proposition 4.0.3, it is enough to show that

$$ g^{\mathbf{v}}(16^{\ell})\geq\frac{1}{8}\left(f^{\mathbf{v}}(16^{\ell})-f^{\mathbf{v}}(16^{\frac{\ell r}{2}})\right). $$

holds for all $\ell\in L.$ In fact, we will prove something stronger. For any $p\leq\frac{1}{16}$ and any $\lambda,\in\Gamma(p),\mu\in\Delta(p),$ there exists some $\sigma\in\Gamma(p^{\frac{r}{2}})$ such that

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}_{S_{i}\longleftarrow\lambda^{i},T_{i}\longleftarrow\mu}[\mathbf{v}^{i}(S_{i}\backslash T_{i})]\geq\frac{1}{8}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}_{S_{i}\longleftarrow\lambda^{i}}[\mathbf{v}^{i}(S_{i})]-\frac{1}{8}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}_{A_{i}\longleftarrow\sigma^{i}}[\mathbf{v}^{i}(A_{i})]. $$

Taking suprema on both sides yields Eq. 4. We prove this fact in similar manner to Proposition 4.0.3. Let $T_{i,u}$ for $1\leq u\leq r$ be $rn$ independent sets from the distribution $\mu.$ Then, for any $i\in[n],$

$$ \mathbf{E}_{S_{i}\longleftarrow\lambda^{i},T_{i}\longleftarrow\mu}[\mathbf{v}^{i}(S_{i}\backslash T_{i})]=\mathbf{E}_{S_{i}\longleftarrow\lambda^{i},T_{i,u}\longleftarrow\mu}\left[\frac{1}{r}\sum_{u=1}^{r}\mathbf{v}^{i}(S_{i}\backslash T_{i,u})\right]. $$

Now, let $A_{i}$ be the set of elements of $S_{i}$ that appear in more than $\frac{7r}{8}$ of the sets $T_{i,1},T_{i,2},\ldots,T_{i,r}.$ Let $\sigma^{i}$ be the distribution of $A_{i}.$ The same reasoning as in Proposition 4.0.3 shows that

$$ \mathbf{E}_{S_{i}\longleftarrow\lambda^{i},T_{i,u}\longleftarrow\mu}\left[\frac{1}{r}\sum_{u=1}^{r}\mathbf{v}^{i}(S_{i}\backslash T_{i,u})\right]\geq\frac{1}{8}\mathbf{E}_{S_{i}\longleftarrow\lambda^{i}}[\mathbf{v}^{i}(S_{i})]-\frac{1}{8}\mathbf{E}_{A_{i}\longleftarrow\sigma^{i}}[\mathbf{v}^{i}(A_{i})]. $$

Thus, summing over $i,$ we conclude that

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}_{S_{i}\longleftarrow\lambda^{i},T_{i}\longleftarrow\mu}[\mathbf{v}^{i}(S_{i}\backslash T_{i})]\geq\frac{1}{8}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}_{S_{i}\longleftarrow\lambda^{i}}[\mathbf{v}^{i}(S_{i})]-\frac{1}{8}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{E}_{A_{i}\longleftarrow\sigma^{i}}[\mathbf{v}^{i}(A_{i})]. $$

To conclude, we simply need to show that $\sigma\in\Gamma(p^{\frac{r}{2}}).$ This holds for the following reason. Take some $j\in[m].$ Define $p_{i}=\mathbf{P}_{S_{i}\longleftarrow\lambda^{i}}[j\in S_{i}].$ By the definition of $\Gamma(p),$ we know that $\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\leq p.$ On the other hand, as each $p_{i}$ satisfies $p_{i}\leq p\leq\frac{1}{16},$ as in Proposition 4.0.3, we conclude that

$$ \mathbf{P}_{A_{i}\longleftarrow\sigma^{i}}[j\in A_{i}]\leq p_{i}^{r/2}. $$

Thus, all we need to show is that

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}^{r/2}\leq p^{r/2}. $$

This, however, is simple. The map $x\longrightarrow x^{r/2}$ is convex. Thus, its maximum on the simplex defined by $0\leq p_{i}\;\forall i\in[n],\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\leq p$ is attained at a vertex. This exactly corresponds to

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}^{r/2}\leq p^{r/2}. $$

∎

The statement we want is a simple corollary of Lemma E.0.2.

#### Lemma E.0.3.

If $\mathcal{D}$ is a product distribution over $q$ -partitioning valuations, there exists some deterministic $p\in[0,1]$ (potentially depending on $\mathcal{D}$ ) such that

$$ \mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{v}}\left[g^{\mathbf{v}}(p)\right]\geq\Omega\left(\frac{\log\log q}{\log\log m}\right)\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{v}}[\mathbf{v}(\mathsf{OPT}(\mathbf{v}))]. $$

#### Proof.

Using the uniform distribution $Unif(L)$ over $L,$ we conclude from Lemma E.0.2 that

$$ \mathbf{E}_{\ell\longleftarrow Unif(L)}[g^{\mathbf{v}}(16^{\ell})]\geq\frac{1}{8s}\left(\frac{1}{16}-\frac{1}{m}\right)\mathbf{v}(\mathsf{OPT}(\mathbf{v})). $$

Taking the expectation over $\mathbf{v}$ and interchanging order of expectations, we obtain

$$ \mathbf{E}_{\ell\longleftarrow Unif(L)}\left[\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{v}}[g^{\mathbf{v}}(16^{\ell})]\right]\geq\frac{1}{8s}\left(\frac{1}{16}-\frac{1}{m}\right)\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{v}}[\mathbf{v}(\mathsf{OPT}(\mathbf{v}))]. $$

Therefore, as $g^{\mathbf{v}}$ is clearly non-negative, the moment method implies the existence of some $\ell_{1}$ such that

$$ \mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{v}}[g^{\mathbf{v}}(16^{\ell_{1}})]\geq\frac{1}{8s}\left(\frac{1}{16}-\frac{1}{m}\right)\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{v}}[\mathbf{v}(\mathsf{OPT}(\mathbf{v}))]. $$

Using that $\frac{1}{s}=\Omega\left(\frac{\log\log q}{\log\log m}\right),$ we complete the proof. ∎

The statement of Theorem 4.0.1 for the incomplete information case follows from Lemma E.0.1 andLemma E.0.3.

## Appendix F Concentration Inequalities

We discuss in full detail the concentration inequalities in Section 5 and their more general versions. The setup that we consider throughout the rest of this section is the following. A valuation $v$ over $[m]$ is given. $S\subseteq[m]$ is a random set such that each item $j\in[m]$ appears independently in $S$ (different items might appear with different probabilities). We study how concentrated $v(S)$ is around a point of interest such as its mean or median. Before delving into the main content, we make one important note. Concentration inequalities and tail bounds depend on the scale of the valuations. That is, the valuation $2v$ has a “weaker” concentration than the valuation $v$ (at least when considering an additive deviation from the mean of the form $\mathbf{E}[v(S)]\pm t$ ). For that reason, throughout we assume that all marginal values, i.e. values $v(S\cup\{i\})-v(S)$ for $S\subseteq[m],i\in[m],$ are between 0 and 1. Note that if $v$ is subadditive, in particular $q$ -partitioning for some $q,$ this is equivalent to $v(\{i\})\leq 1\;\forall i\in[m]$ .

Throughout the rest of the section, by abuse of notation, we will write $v(S)$ and $v(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{m})$ interchangeably where $(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{m})$ is the characteristic vector of $S$ in $\{0,1\}^{m}.$

### F.1 Concentration via Self-Bounding Functions

Vondrak shows that XOS and submodular functions exhibit strong concentration via self-bounding functions [Von10, Corollary 3.2]. We adopt this approach and show how the bounds generalize to MPH- $k$ valuations with bounded marginal values and, in particular, to $q$ -partitioning valuations (naturally, the concentration becomes weaker as $q$ decreases). This approach relies on the method of self-bounding functions.

#### Definition F.1.1 ( [Von10, Definition 2.3]).

A function $f:\{0,1\}^{m}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is $(a,b)$ -self-bounding if there exist real numbers $a,b>0$ and functions $f_{i}:\{0,1\}^{m-1}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ such that if we denote $x^{(i)}=(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{i-1},x_{i+1},\ldots,x_{m}),$ then for all $x\in\{0,1\}^{m}$ and $i\in[m]:$

$$ 0\leq f(x)-f_{i}(x^{(i)})\leq 1,\text{ and } $$

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{m}(f(x)-f_{i}(x^{(i)}))\leq af(x)+b. $$

When $f$ is monotone, the optimal choice of $f_{i}$ is clearly given by $f_{i}(x^{(i)}):=f(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{i-1},0,x_{i+1},\ldots,x_{m}).$ We adopt this approach in Proposition F.1.3. An application of the entropy method gives the following concentration for self-bounding functions.

#### Theorem F.1.2 ([Von10, Theorem 3.3]).

If $f:\{0,1\}^{m}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is $(a,b)$ -self-bounding for some $a\geq\frac{1}{3},$ and $X_{1},X_{2},\ldots,X_{m}$ are independent, then for $Z=f(X_{1},X_{2},\ldots,X_{m})$ and $c=\frac{3a-1}{6}:$

$$ \begin{split}&\mathbf{P}[Z\geq\mathbf{E}[Z]+t]\leq\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\times\frac{t^{2}}{a\mathbf{E}[Z]+b+ct}\right)\;\text{ for any }0<t,\\
&\mathbf{P}[Z\leq\mathbf{E}[Z]-t]\leq\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\times\frac{t^{2}}{a\mathbf{E}[Z]+b}\right)\;\text{ for any }0<t<\mathbf{E}[Z].\end{split} $$

Vondrak [Von10, Lemma 2.2] shows that XOS valuations (also $m$ -partitioning or MPH-1) are $(1,0)$ -self-bounding. We generalize as follows.

#### Proposition F.1.3.

Any (not necessarily subadditive) MPH- $k$ valuation with all marginal values in $[0,1]$ is $(k,0)$ -self-bounding. In particular, this holds for all subadditive MPH- $k$ valuations $f$ such that $f(\{i\})\leq 1\;\forall i\in[m].$

#### Proof.

We make the canonical choice $f_{i}(x^{(i)}):=(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{i-1},0,x_{i+1},\ldots,x_{n})$ in the proof. In other words, $f_{i}(S):=f(S\backslash\{i\}).$ Note that $0\leq f(x)-f_{i}(x^{(i)})\leq 1$ follows from the fact that $f$ is monotone and all marginal values are bounded by 1. We need to prove that for any $S\subseteq[m],$ it is the case that

$$ \sum_{j\in[m]}(f(S)-f(S\backslash\{j\}))\leq kf(S) $$

The latter is clearly equivalent to

$$ \sum_{j\in S}(f(S)-f(S\backslash\{j\}))\leq kf(S), $$

which is the statement of [Ezr+19, Lemma 6.2]. ∎

Combining the above propositions with Proposition 3.2.3, we immediately deduce Theorem 5.0.1.

Note that this result is potentially useful only when $\mathbf{E}[v(S)]\ll q.$ Otherwise Azuma’s inequality [VW18] implies that $v(S)$ is $m$ -subgaussian. In fact, this holds for any 1-Lipschitz (not necessarily subadditive!) function $f:\{0,1\}^{m}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}.$

So, can we derive any tail bounds for small values of $q$ (in particular, subadditive valuations) which are better than what is already true for any $1$ -Lipschitz valuations over $[m]$ ? It turns out that the answer to this question is “yes” and this is the subject of the next section. Before turning to it, however, we note that we cannot hope to do much better than Theorem 5.0.1 using the method of self-bounding functions.

#### Example F.1.4.

For any $2\leq q\leq m,$ there exists a symmetric $q$ -partitioning valuation over $[m]$ with marginal values in $[0,1]$ which is not $(a,0)$ -self-bounding for any $a<\frac{m}{q}.$ Indeed, consider the $q$ -partitioning function $v$ constructed in Proposition 3.0.3, defined by $v(\emptyset)=0,v(S)=1$ for $\emptyset\subsetneq S\subsetneq[m],$ and $v([m])=\frac{q}{q-1}.$ Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that $v$ is $(a,0)$ -self-bounding for some $a<\frac{m}{q}$ and $v_{i}.$ Then, for any $S$ with characteristic vector $x$ and $i\in[m],$ it must be the case that $v_{i}(x^{(i)})\leq f(S\backslash\{i\})\leq 1$ by the first inequality in Definition F.1.1. As a result, when we set $x$ to be the all-ones vector in the second inequality, we conclude that $a\frac{q}{q-1}\geq\frac{m}{q-1}.$ Thus, $a\geq\frac{m}{q},$ which is a contradiction.

### F.2 Tail Bounds via an Isoperimetric Inequality

We now take a deeper look into the stated isoperimetric inequalities in Section 5. To do so, we first present some background on Theorem 5.1.1 and the proof of the statement.

#### F.2.1 The Isoperimetric Inequality

We consider the setup introduced in Section 5.1. In [Tal01, Section 3.1.1] the author considers the special case $s=1,$ and in [Tal96, Section 5.7] he considers the special case $s=q-1.$ In particular, the inequalities he proves are the following.

#### Theorem F.2.1 ([Tal01, Section 3.2]).

Suppose that $\alpha>0$ is a real number and $z(q,\alpha)$ is the larger root of the equation $z+q\alpha z^{-\frac{1}{\alpha}}=1+q\alpha.$ Then

$$ \int_{\Omega}z(q,\alpha)^{f^{1}(A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{q};x)}d\mathbf{P}(x)\leq\frac{1}{\prod_{i=1}^{q}\mathbf{P}[A_{i}]^{\alpha}}. $$

In particular, setting $A=A_{1}=A_{2}=\ldots=A_{q},\alpha=1,z=q,$ one has

$$ \mathbf{P}[f^{1}(\underbrace{A,A,\ldots,A}_{q};x)\geq k]\leq q^{-k}\mathbf{P}[A]^{-q}. $$

Theorem F.2.1 is the main tool in Schechtman’s bound (see Section 5). The result for $s=q-1$ looks similar:

#### Theorem F.2.2.

([Tal96, Theorem 5.4]) Suppose that $\tau$ is the positive root of $e^{\tau/2}+e^{-\tau}=2.$ Then,

$$ \int_{\Omega}e^{\frac{\tau}{q}f^{q-1}(A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{q};x)}d\mathbf{P}(x)\leq\frac{1}{\prod_{i=1}^{q}\mathbf{P}[A_{i}]^{1/q}}. $$

In particular, setting $A=A_{1}=A_{2}=\ldots=A_{q}$ one has

$$ \mathbf{P}[f^{q-1}(\underbrace{A,A,\ldots,A}_{q};x)\geq k]\leq e^{-\frac{\tau k}{q}}\mathbf{P}[A]^{-1}. $$

In this section, we provide a uniform view on Theorem F.2.1 and Theorem F.2.2 by proving Theorem 5.1.1. First, we will demystify the number $t(\alpha,q,s).$ It comes from the following fact.

#### Lemma F.2.3.

Suppose that $x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{q}$ are real numbers in $[0,1]$ and $\alpha\geq\frac{1}{s}.$ Then, for $t(\alpha,q,s)$ defined as in Theorem 5.1.1, one has

$$ \min\left(t(\alpha,q,s),\min_{1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{s}\leq q}(x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\cdots x_{i_{s}})^{-\alpha}\right)+\alpha\sum_{i=1}^{q}x_{i}\leq\alpha q+1. $$

Furthermore, $t(\alpha,q,s)$ is the largest $t$ with this property. We use the convention that $0^{-\alpha}=+\infty.$

As the proof of Lemma F.2.3 provides no insight and is just a computation, we postpone it to Section F.3. We also remark that a version of Theorem 5.1.1 holds for $\alpha<\frac{1}{s}$ as well, but the definition of $t(\alpha,q,s)$ becomes even more complicated (see Remark F.3.1). We now turn to the proof of Theorem 5.1.1.

#### Proof of Theorem 5.1.1.

We follow closely the proof of Theorem F.2.2 due to Talagrand in [Tal96]. We proceed by induction over $N,$ the dimension of the product space.

Base: When $N=1,$ let $g_{i}$ be the indicator function of $A_{i}$ for $1\leq i\leq q.$ Observe that

$$ \int_{\Omega}t(\alpha,q,s)^{f^{s}(A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{q};x)}d\mathbf{P}(x)= $$

$$ \int_{\Omega}\min\left(t(\alpha,q,s),\min_{1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{s}\leq q}(g_{i_{1}}(x)g_{i_{2}}(x)\cdots g_{i_{s}}(x))^{-\alpha}\right)d\mathbf{P}(x). $$

Indeed, this is true because $f^{s}(A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{q};x)=0$ when there exist $s$ sets $A_{i_{1}},A_{i_{2}},\ldots,A_{i_{s}}$ to which $x$ belongs and $f^{s}(A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{q};x)=1$ otherwise simply by the definition $f^{s}.$ Using Lemma F.2.3, we conclude that

$$ \int_{\Omega}\min\left(t(\alpha,q,s),\min_{1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{s}\leq q}(g_{i_{1}}(x)g_{i_{2}}(x)\cdots g_{i_{s}}(x))^{-\alpha}\right)d\mathbf{P}(x)\leq $$

$$ 1+\alpha q-\alpha\sum_{i=1}^{q}\int_{\Omega}g_{i}(x)d\mathbf{P}(x)=1+\alpha q-\alpha\sum_{i=1}^{q}\mathbf{P}[A_{i}]. $$

Now, we will use twice the well known inequality $1+\log x\leq x$ as follows

$$ 1+\alpha q-\alpha\sum_{i=1}^{q}\mathbf{P}[A_{i}]=1+\alpha\sum_{i=1}^{q}(1-\mathbf{P}[A_{i}])\leq 1+\alpha\sum_{i=1}^{q}\log\frac{1}{\mathbf{P}[A_{i}]}= $$

$$ 1+\log\prod_{i=1}^{q}\frac{1}{\mathbf{P}[A_{i}]^{\alpha}}\leq\prod_{i=1}^{q}\frac{1}{\mathbf{P}[A_{i}]^{\alpha}}, $$

with which the base case is completed.

Inductive Step: Now, let $A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{q}$ all belong to $\Omega=\Omega^{\prime}\times\Omega_{N+1},$ where $\Omega^{\prime}=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\Omega_{i}.$ For each $i\in[q],w\in\Omega_{N+1}$ define the following sets:

$$ A_{i}(w)=\{x\in\Omega^{\prime}\;:\;(x,w)\in A_{i}\}, $$

$$ B_{i}=\bigcup_{w\in\Omega_{N+1}}A_{i}(w). $$

Fix some $w\in\Omega_{N+1}.$ For $I\subseteq[q]$ with $|I|=s,$ denote $C^{I}_{i}=A_{i}(w)$ whenever $i\in I$ and $C^{I}_{i}=B_{i}$ whenever $i\not\in I.$ Then, we can make the following observations:

$$ f^{s}(A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{q};(x,w))\leq 1+f^{s}(B_{1},B_{2},\ldots,B_{q};x)\;\forall(x,w)\in\Omega, $$

$$ f^{s}(A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{q};(x,w))\leq f^{s}(C^{I}_{1},C^{I}_{2},\ldots,C^{I}_{q};x)\;\forall(x,w)\in\Omega,I\subseteq[q]\text{ with }|I|=s. $$

Indeed, the first inequality follows from the following fact. If $(b^{1},b^{2},\ldots,b^{q})\in B_{1}\times B_{2}\times\cdots\times B_{q},$ then for each $i,$ we can find some $a^{i}=(b^{i},w^{i})\in A_{i}.$ Clearly,

$$ f^{s}(a^{1},a^{2},\ldots,a^{q};(x,w))\leq 1+f^{s}(b^{1},b^{2},\ldots,b^{q};x) $$

as the only extra coordinate that may appear less than $s$ times in the required multiset in Eq. 3 is the $N+1$ ’th coordinate $w.$ The second inequality follows from the same fact except that we choose $a^{i}=(b^{i},w)$ whenever $i\in I.$

Having those two inequalities, we can fix $w$ and compute:

$$ \int_{\Omega^{\prime}}t(\alpha,q,s)^{f^{s}(A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{q};(x,w))}d\mathbf{P}(x)\leq $$

$$ \int_{\Omega^{\prime}}\min\left(t(\alpha,q,s)^{1+f^{s}(B_{1},B_{2},\ldots,B_{q};x)},\min_{{}_{|I|=s}}t(\alpha,q,s)^{f^{s}(C^{I}_{1},C^{I}_{2},\ldots,C^{I}_{q};x)}\right)\leq $$

$$ \min\left(\int_{\Omega^{\prime}}t(\alpha,q,s)^{1+f^{s}(B_{1},B_{2},\ldots,B_{q};x)},\min_{{}_{|I|=s}}\int_{\Omega^{\prime}}t(\alpha,q,s)^{f^{s}(C^{I}_{1},C^{I}_{2},\ldots,C^{I}_{q};x)}\right). $$

Now, we just use the inductive hypothesis as each $B_{i}$ and $C^{I}_{i}$ is in the space $\Omega^{\prime},$ which is a product of $N$ spaces. We bound the above expression by

$$ \min\left(t(\alpha,q,s)\frac{1}{\prod_{i=1}^{q}\mathbf{P}[B_{i}]^{\alpha}},\min_{|I|=s}\frac{1}{\prod_{i=1}^{q}\mathbf{P}[C^{I}_{i}]^{\alpha}}\right)= $$

$$ \frac{1}{\prod_{i=1}^{q}\mathbf{P}[B_{i}]^{\alpha}}\min\left(t(\alpha,q,s),\min_{1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<\ldots<i_{s}\leq q}\frac{\mathbf{P}[B_{i_{1}}]^{\alpha}}{\mathbf{P}[A_{i_{1}}(w)]^{\alpha}}\frac{\mathbf{P}[B_{i_{2}}]^{\alpha}}{\mathbf{P}[A_{i_{2}}(w)]^{\alpha}}\cdots\frac{\mathbf{P}[B_{i_{s}}]^{\alpha}}{\mathbf{P}[A_{i_{s}}(w)]^{\alpha}}\right)\leq $$

$$ \frac{1}{\prod_{i=1}^{q}\mathbf{P}[B_{i}]^{\alpha}}\left(1+\alpha q-\alpha\sum_{i=1}^{q}\frac{\mathbf{P}[A_{i}(w)]}{\mathbf{P}[B_{i}]}\right), $$

where in the last inequality we used Lemma F.2.3 since $\frac{\mathbf{P}[A_{i}(w)]}{\mathbf{P}[B_{i}]}\leq 1$ for each $i.$ However, as we are dealing with a product measure, by Tonelli’s theorem for non-negative functions, it follows that

$$ \int_{\Omega}t(\alpha,q,s)^{f^{s}(A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{q};(x,w))}d\mathbf{P}(x,w)= $$

$$ \int_{\Omega_{n+1}}\int_{\Omega^{\prime}}t(\alpha,q,s)^{f^{s}(A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{q};(x,w))}d\mathbf{P}(x)d\mathbf{P}(w)\leq $$

$$ \int_{\Omega_{n+1}}\frac{1}{\prod_{i=1}^{q}\mathbf{P}[B_{i}]^{\alpha}}\left(1+\alpha q-\alpha\sum_{i=1}^{q}\frac{\mathbf{P}[A_{i}(w)]}{\mathbf{P}[B_{i}]}\right)d\mathbf{P}(w)= $$

$$ \frac{1}{\prod_{i=1}^{q}\mathbf{P}[B_{i}]^{\alpha}}\int_{\Omega_{n+1}}\left(1+\alpha q-\alpha\sum_{i=1}^{q}\frac{\mathbf{P}[A_{i}(w)]}{\mathbf{P}[B_{i}]}\right)d\mathbf{P}(w). $$

Using the same approach as in the base case, but this time for the functions $g_{i}(w):=\frac{\mathbf{P}[A_{i}(w)])}{\mathbf{P}[B_{i}]},$ we bound the last expression by

$$ \frac{1}{\prod_{i=1}^{q}\mathbf{P}[B_{i}]^{\alpha}}\times\frac{1}{\prod_{i=1}^{q}\left(\frac{\mathbf{P}[A_{i}]}{\mathbf{P}[B_{i}]}\right)^{\alpha}}=\frac{1}{\prod_{i=1}^{q}\mathbf{P}[A_{i}]^{\alpha}}, $$

as desired. ∎

#### F.2.2 Tail Bounds and Median-Mean Inequalities for q-Partitioning Valuations

We first begin with a generalization of Theorem 5.0.2, which has the same proof.

#### Theorem F.2.4.

Suppose that $v$ is a $q$ -partitioning valuation over $[m],$ and $S\subseteq[m]$ is a random set in which each element appears independently. Then the following inequality holds for any $a\geq 0,k\geq 0,$ $s,r\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $1\leq s<r\leq\log_{2}q,$ and $\alpha\geq\frac{1}{s}:$

$$ \mathbf{P}[v(S)\geq\frac{r}{s}a+k]\leq t(\alpha,r,s)^{-k}\mathbf{P}[v(S)\leq a]^{-\alpha r}. $$

In particular, choosing $a$ to be the median, $\alpha=\frac{1}{s},t(\alpha,r,s)=\frac{r}{s},$ we recover Theorem 5.0.2.

Note that in the proof of Theorem 5.0.2, we only needed $r\leq\log_{2}q$ to ensure that the sets $M_{1},M_{2},\ldots,M_{r}$ “split” $[m]$ into at most $q$ parts. This assumption, however, is unnecessary if $v$ is XOS (or $q=m$ ) as one cannot “split” $[m]$ into more than $m$ parts. This gives rise to even more “fine-grained” inequalities in the XOS case. To present them, however, we will make a slight change of notation. Before, we defined $t(\alpha,r,s)$ as the larger root of $t+\alpha rt^{-\frac{1}{\alpha s}}=\alpha r+1.$ We can take $r$ and $s$ to be arbitrary integers satisfying $r>s$ when $v$ is XOS as discussed. Thus, the ratio $\frac{r}{s}$ can approximate an arbitrary real number $1+\delta>1.$ With this in mind, we make the following twist. Denote by $\xi(\psi,\delta)$ the larger root of the equation $\xi+\psi\xi^{-\frac{1+\delta}{\psi}}=\psi+1$ for some $\psi\geq 1+\delta>1.$ This is essentially the same equation after the substitution $\psi=\alpha r,1+\delta=\frac{r}{s}.$ The condition $\alpha\geq\frac{1}{s}$ is equivalent to $\psi\geq 1+\delta.$ We have:

#### Theorem F.2.5.

Suppose that $v$ is a valuation over $[m]$ that is $\beta$ -close (in the sense of Definition 3.0.4) to being XOS and $S\subseteq[m]$ is a random set in which each element appears independently. Then the following inequality holds for any real numbers $\psi\geq 1+\delta>1,a>0,k\geq 0$

$$ \mathbf{P}[v(S)\geq\frac{(1+\delta)}{\beta}a+k]\leq\xi(\psi,\delta)^{-k}\mathbf{P}[v(S)\leq a]^{-\psi}. $$

In particular, choosing $a$ to be the median, $\psi=1+\delta,\xi=1+\delta$ the inequality becomes

$$ \mathbf{P}[v(S)\geq\frac{(1+\delta)}{\beta}a+k]\leq\left(1+\delta\right)^{-k}2^{1+\delta}. $$

#### Proof.

The proof is analogous to the one of Theorem F.2.4, except that this time we have

$$ \beta v(T\backslash M)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}\frac{1}{s}v(M_{i})\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}\frac{1}{s}v(T_{i})=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\frac{1}{s}v(y^{i})\leq\frac{ra}{s} $$

as $v$ is $\beta$ -close to being XOS. ∎

We end with a discussion of median-mean inequalities, which are part of the motivation for our endeavour in this section. Namely, in [RW18], the authors use the following crucial property of 1-Lipschitz subadditive valuations. Using Schechtman’s bound (see Section 5), they obtain $\mathbf{E}[v(S)]\leq 3\mathbf{Med}[v(S)]+O(1).$ We generalize this as follows.

#### Proposition F.2.6.

Suppose that the non-negative random variable $Z$ satisfies the following inequality for some $0<\delta\leq 1,$ and any $k>0.$

$$ \mathbf{P}[Z\geq(1+\delta)\mathbf{Med}[Z]+k]\leq(1+\delta)^{-k}2^{1+\delta}. $$

Then, $\mathbf{E}[Z]\leq(1+\delta)\mathbf{Med}[Z]+O(\frac{1}{\delta}).$

#### Proof.

Let $k$ be some non-negative real number that we will chose later. Then,

$$ \mathbf{E}[Z]=\int_{0}^{+\infty}\mathbf{P}[Z\geq t]\leq(1+\delta)\mathbf{Med}[Z]+k+\int_{k}^{+\infty}\mathbf{P}[Z\geq(1+\delta)\mathbf{Med}[Z]+t]dt\leq $$

$$ (1+\delta)\mathbf{Med}[Z]+k+\int_{k}^{+\infty}2^{1+\delta}(1+\delta)^{-t}dt=(1+\delta)\mathbf{Med}[Z]+k+2^{1+\delta}\frac{1}{\ln(1+\delta)}(1+\delta)^{-k}. $$

Choosing $k=\frac{1}{\ln(1+\delta)}$ and using the inequality $0<\delta\leq 1,$ which also implies $\frac{\delta}{2}\leq\frac{1}{\ln(1+\delta)}\leq\delta,$ we bound the above expression by

$$ (1+\delta)\mathbf{Med}[Z]+O\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right). $$

∎

Applying this statement to $q$ -partitioning valuations, we obtain the following two corollaries.

#### Corollary F.2.7.

If $v$ is $q$ -partitioning, then $\mathbf{E}[v(S)]\leq(1+O(\frac{1}{\log q}))\mathbf{Med}[v(S)]+O(\log q).$

#### Proof.

We just apply Proposition F.2.6 for $\delta=\frac{1}{\lceil\log q\rceil}$ and combine with Theorem F.2.4. ∎

#### Corollary F.2.8.

If $v$ is XOS, then $\mathbf{E}[V(S)]\leq\mathbf{Med}[v(S)]+O(\sqrt{\mathbf{Med}[v(S)]}).$

#### Proof.

We apply Proposition F.2.6 with $\delta=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathbf{Med}[v(S)]}}$ and combine with Theorem F.2.5. ∎

Note that the last result matches the state-of-the-art median-mean bound for XOS function implied by the $\mathbf{E}[v(S)]$ -subgaussian behaviour of $v.$ Indeed, the lower tail-bound in Theorem 5.0.1 for $v$ XOS implies that $\mathbf{Med}[v(S)]\geq\mathbf{E}[v(S)]-O(\sqrt{\mathbf{E}[v(S)]}).$ More generally, median-mean bounds can also be derived using Theorem 5.0.1, but are only useful for large $q$ unlike Corollary F.2.7. Namely, $\mathbf{Med}[v(S)]\geq\mathbf{E}[v(S)]-O(\sqrt{\frac{m}{q}\mathbf{E}[v(S)]})$ holds for $q$ -partitioning valuations.

### F.3 Technical Details

We omitted the proof of Lemma F.2.3. We give this proof here. First, however, we need to show that the equation $t+\alpha qt^{-\frac{1}{\alpha s}}=\alpha q+1$ has two positive roots and one of them is larger than 1. Clearly, $t=1$ is a root. Denote $f(t):=t+\alpha qt^{-\frac{1}{\alpha s}}-\alpha q-1.$ Note that $f^{\prime}(t)=1-\frac{q}{s}t^{-1-\frac{1}{\alpha s}}.$ As $q>s,$ $f^{\prime}$ has a single root $t_{0}=\left(\frac{q}{s}\right)^{\frac{\alpha s}{\alpha s+1}}$ and this root is larger than $1$ (but smaller than $\frac{q}{s}$ ). Thus, $f^{\prime}$ is decreasing in $(0,t_{0})$ and increasing in $[t_{0},+\infty).$ Therefore, $f(t_{0})<f(1)=0.$ Since $\lim_{t\longrightarrow+\infty}f(t)=+\infty,$ $f$ has just one more root and this root is larger than $1.$ We can now proceed to the proof of Lemma F.2.3.

#### Proof of Lemma F.2.3.

Without loss of generality, let $0\leq x_{1}\leq x_{2}\leq\ldots\leq x_{q}\leq 1.$ Thus, we need to prove that

$$ \min\left(t(\alpha,q,s),(x_{q-s+1}x_{q-s+2}\cdots x_{q})^{-\alpha}\right)+\alpha\sum_{i=1}^{q}x_{i}\leq\alpha q+1. $$

Note that we can assume that $(x_{q-s+1}x_{q-s+2}\cdots x_{q})^{-\alpha}\leq t(\alpha,q,s).$ Indeed, otherwise we can increase the numbers $x_{q-s+1},x_{q-s+2},\ldots,x_{q}$ until this inequality is satisfied and the left hand-side will only increase. Now, on, we will assume that $B=(x_{q-s+1}x_{q-s+2}\cdots x_{q})^{-\alpha}\leq t(\alpha,q,s).$

Similarly note that we can assume that $x_{1}=x_{2}=\cdots=x_{q-s+1}.$

Now, keeping $x_{q-s+1}$ fixed and $x_{q-s+1}x_{q-s+2}\cdots x_{q}$ fixed, note that the sum $\sum_{i=q-s+1}^{q}x_{i}$ is maximized when there exists some $0\leq r\leq s$ such that

$$ 1=x_{q}=x_{q-1}=\cdots=x_{q-r+1}\geq x_{q-r}\geq x_{q-r-1}=x_{g-r-2}=\cdots=x_{q-s+1}. $$

This is indeed the case since when we keep the product of two numbers $a\leq b$ fixed, their sum increases as they get further apart. Formally, $a\gamma+b\gamma^{-1}\geq a+b$ for any $0<\gamma<1.$

Under these assumptions, denote $y=x_{q-r}$ and $x_{q-r-1}=x_{g-r-2}=\cdots=x_{q-s+1}=x.$ Using this notation, we want to maximize

$$ h(x,y)=(yx^{s-r-1})^{-\alpha}+\alpha(r+y+(s-r-1)x) $$

in the set $\mathcal{K}=\{(x,y)>0\;:\;(yx^{s-r-1})^{-\alpha}\leq t(\alpha,q,s)\text{ and }0\leq x\leq y\leq 1\}.$ Note that $\mathcal{K}$ is compact and $h$ is continuous. Therefore, there exists a maximizer. We can easily see that this maximizer is not in the interior of $\mathcal{K}$ as $\nabla_{y}h=\alpha-\alpha y^{-\alpha-1}x^{-\alpha(s-r-1)}<0$ in the interior. Thus, the gradient is non-zero and by moving in the direction of the gradient, the value of $h$ will increase. Thus, all the maximizers are on the boundary. There are three cases to consider: Case 1) $y=x.$ Then, we need to prove that

$$ x^{-\alpha(s-r)}+\alpha(r+(q-r)x)\leq\alpha q+1 $$

whenever $0\leq r\leq s$ and $x^{-\alpha(s-r)}\leq t(\alpha,q,s).$ First, note that if $s=r,$ the inequality is trivial. For that reason, we assume that $0\leq r<s-1$ now on. Consider the function

$$ g(x)=x^{-\alpha(s-r)}+\alpha(r+(q-r)x)-\alpha q-1. $$

Then,

$$ g^{\prime}(x)=-\alpha(s-r)x^{-\alpha(s-r)-1}+(q-r), $$

so the function $g^{\prime}$ has exactly one positive root $x_{0}.$ It follows that $g$ is decreasing in $(0,x_{0})$ and increasing in $(x_{0},+\infty).$ No matter what the value of $x_{0}$ is, this means that the maximal value of $g$ on $[t(\alpha,q,s)^{-\frac{1}{\alpha(s-r)}},1]$ (which is the set of feasible values for $x$ ) is always at either the point $1$ or the point $t(\alpha,q,s)^{-\frac{1}{\alpha(s-r)}}.$ Thus, we simply need to prove that $g(1)\leq 0$ and $g(t(\alpha,q,s)^{-\frac{1}{\alpha(s-r)}})\leq 0.$ The first inequality is trivial. The second is equivalent to:

$$ t(\alpha,q,s)+\alpha r+\alpha(q-r)t(\alpha,q,s)^{-\frac{1}{\alpha(s-r)}}\leq\alpha q+1\Longleftrightarrow $$

$$ t(\alpha,q,s)^{-\frac{1}{\alpha(s-r)}}\leq\frac{\alpha(q-r)+1-t(\alpha,q,s)}{\alpha(q-r)}. $$

Note that for this inequality to hold, we first need to prove that $\alpha(q-r)+1-t(\alpha,q,s)\geq 0.$ In fact, we will prove that $\alpha(q-s)+1\geq t(\alpha,q,s).$ Since $\alpha\geq\frac{1}{s},$ we see that $\alpha(q-s)+1\geq\frac{q}{s}\geq t_{0},$ where $t_{0}$ is the root of the derivative of $f(t)=t+\alpha qt^{-\frac{1}{\alpha s}},$ defined in the beginning of this appendix. Since $f$ is increasing on $[t_{0},+\infty),$ all we need to prove is that

$$ f(\alpha(q-s)+1)\geq f(t({\alpha,q,s}))=0\Longleftrightarrow $$

$$ (1+\alpha(q-s))+\alpha q(1+\alpha(q-s))^{-\frac{1}{\alpha s}}\geq\alpha q+1\Longleftrightarrow $$

$$ \alpha q(1+\alpha(q-s))^{-\frac{1}{\alpha s}}\geq\alpha s\Longleftrightarrow $$

$$ (1+\alpha(q-s))^{-\frac{1}{\alpha s}}\geq\frac{s}{q}\Longleftrightarrow $$

$$ (1+\alpha(q-s))^{\frac{1}{\alpha s}}\leq\frac{q}{s}. $$

However, as $\frac{1}{\alpha s}\leq 1$ by the choice of $\alpha,$ by the famous Bernoulli inequality, we know that

$$ (1+\alpha(q-s))^{\frac{1}{\alpha s}}\leq 1+\frac{\alpha(q-s)}{\alpha s}=\frac{q}{s}, $$

as desired.

Now that we know $\frac{\alpha(q-r)+1-t(\alpha,q,s)}{\alpha(q-r)}\geq 0,$ the desired inequality becomes equivalent to proving

$$ t(\alpha,q,s)^{-\frac{1}{\alpha s}}\leq\left(\frac{\alpha(q-r)+1-t(\alpha,q,s)}{\alpha(q-r)}\right)^{\frac{s-r}{s}}. $$

Using that $t(\alpha,q,s)^{-\frac{1}{\alpha s}}=\frac{\alpha q+1-t(\alpha,q,s)}{\alpha q},$ the above inequality becomes equivalent to

$$ \frac{\alpha q+1-t(\alpha,q,s)}{\alpha q}\leq\left(\frac{\alpha(q-r)+1-t(\alpha,q,s)}{\alpha(q-r)}\right)^{\frac{s-r}{s}}\Longleftrightarrow $$

$$ \left(\frac{\alpha q+1-t(\alpha,q,s)}{\alpha q}\right)^{\alpha s}\leq\left(\frac{\alpha(q-r)+1-t(\alpha,q,s)}{\alpha(q-r)}\right)^{\alpha(s-r)}. $$

To prove this inequality, denote by $b=\alpha(q-s)+1-t(\alpha,q,s)\geq 0,a=t(\alpha,q,s)-1>0.$ Then, we want to prove that

$$ \left(\frac{b+\alpha s}{a+b+\alpha s}\right)^{\alpha s}\leq\left(\frac{b+\alpha(s-r)}{a+b+\alpha(s-r)}\right)^{\alpha(s-r)}. $$

To prove this, we simply show that the function

$$ x\longrightarrow\left(\frac{b+x}{a+b+x}\right)^{x} $$

is decreasing. Equivalently, we want to show that its logarithm $k(x)=x\ln\left(\frac{b+x}{a+b+x}\right)$ is decreasing. This, however, is simple as

$$ k^{\prime}(x)=\ln\left(\frac{b+x}{a+b+x}\right)+x\frac{a+b+x}{b+x}\frac{a}{(a+b+x)^{2}}= $$

$$ \ln\left(\frac{b+x}{a+b+x}\right)+\frac{x}{b+x}\frac{a}{a+b+x}\leq $$

$$ \ln\left(\frac{b+x}{a+b+x}\right)+\frac{a}{a+b+x}=\ln\left(\frac{b+x}{a+b+x}\right)+1-\left(\frac{b+x}{a+b+x}\right)\leq 0, $$

as $\ln(y)+1-y\leq 0$ for all $y.$ With this, case 1 is complete. Case 2) $y=1.$ This is the same case as $1$ except that we replace $r$ with $r-1.$ Case 3) $(yx^{s-r-1})^{-\alpha}=t(\alpha,q,s).$ Then, we know that $y=t(\alpha,q,s)^{-\frac{1}{\alpha}}x^{-(s-r-1)}.$ We need to prove that

$$ t(\alpha,q,s)+\alpha r+\alpha(q-r-1)x+\alpha t(\alpha,q,s)^{-\frac{1}{\alpha}}x^{-(s-r-1)}\leq\alpha q+1. $$

Consider the function $m(x)=\alpha(q-r-1)x+\alpha t(\alpha,q,s)^{-\frac{1}{\alpha}}x^{-(s-r-1)}.$ Then

$$ m^{\prime}(x)=\alpha(q-r-1)-\alpha t(\alpha,q,s)^{-\frac{1}{\alpha}}(s-r-1)x^{-(s-r)}. $$

Note that this function has a unique root $x_{0}.$ Therefore, $m$ is decreasing on $(0,x_{0}]$ and increasing on $[x_{0},+\infty).$ In other words, the maximal values of $m(x)$ on $[t(\alpha,q,s)^{-\frac{1}{\alpha(s-r-1)}},t(\alpha,q,s)^{-\frac{1}{\alpha(s-r)}}]$ (which is the feasible set for $x$ as $x^{-\alpha(s-r-1)}\leq(yx^{s-r-1})^{-\alpha}=t(\alpha,q,s)$ and $x^{-\alpha(s-r)}\geq(yx^{s-r-1})^{-\alpha}=t(\alpha,q,s)$ ) are at the two points $x=t(\alpha,q,s)^{-\frac{1}{\alpha(s-r-1)}}$ and $x=t(\alpha,q,s)^{-\frac{1}{\alpha(s-r)}}.$ However, these cases correspond to $y=1$ and $y=x,$ which were already analyzed in case 1 and case 2.

Finally, we want to prove that the choice of $t$ is optimal. This follows simply by taking $x_{1}=x_{2}=\cdots=x_{q}=t^{-\frac{1}{\alpha s}}.$ ∎

#### Remark F.3.1.

We end this appendix with the remark that one can also obtain similar inequalities when $\alpha<\frac{1}{s},$ but with a potentially different choice of $t.$ Namely, suppose that $\alpha>0$ and $t^{min}(\alpha,q,s)$ is the smallest number among $t_{0},t_{1},\ldots,t_{s-1},$ where $t_{r}$ is the larger root of $t+\alpha(q-r)t^{-\frac{1}{\alpha(s-r)}}=\alpha(q-r)+1.$ From the proof of Lemma F.2.3, it follows that when $\alpha\geq\frac{1}{s},$ it is the case that $t^{min}(\alpha,q,s)=t_{0}=t(\alpha,q,s).$ This, however, might not be the case in general. For example, we can compute that when $q=5,s=2,\alpha=\frac{1}{10},$ we have $t_{0}\approx 1.41,t_{1}\approx 1.38,$ so $t(\alpha,q,s)=t_{0}\neq\min(t_{0},t_{1})=t^{min}(\alpha,q,s).$

With this in mind, the same proofs show that Lemma F.2.3 holds with the value $t^{min}(\alpha,q,s)$ instead of $t(\alpha,q,s)$ for any $\alpha>0.$ Similarly, Theorem 5.1.1 holds with the value $t^{min}(\alpha,q,s)$ instead of $t(\alpha,q,s)$ for any $\alpha>0.$ We did not state the result in this more general form earlier as we specifically wanted to derive the inequalities for $\alpha=\frac{1}{s},t(\alpha,q,s)=\frac{q}{s}.$

## Appendix G Distance to Subadditive Valuations

We will show that subadditive valuations over $[m]$ are $\Omega(\frac{1}{\log q})$ -close to $q$ -partitioning valuations over $[m]$ and this factor is asymptotically tight. Both directions follow closely the framework for XOS approximations of subadditive valuations in [BR11]. Denote by $\mathcal{H}_{a}$ the $a$ -th harmonic number, i.e. $\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{a}=\sum_{i=1}^{a}\frac{1}{i}=\ln a+O(1).$

#### Proposition G.0.1.

$\mathcal{Q}(2,[m])$ is $\frac{1}{\mathcal{H}_{q-1}}$ -close to $\mathcal{Q}(q,[m]).$

#### Proof.

Take any subadditive valuation $g$ over $[m].$ Upon taking the dual of the linear program in Definition 3.0.4, we need to prove the following fact. For any $S\subseteq[m]$ and any partition of $S$ into $q$ parts $S_{1},S_{2},\ldots,S_{q},$ the optimal value of the following linear program

$$ \begin{split}\max\;&\sum_{j\in[q]}p_{j}\text{ s.t.,}\\
&\sum_{j\in I}p_{j}\leq g(\bigcup_{j\in I}S_{j})\;\forall I\subseteq[q],\\
&p_{j}\geq 0\;\forall j\in[q]\end{split} $$

is at least $g(S)/\mathcal{H}_{q-1}.$ We construct the price vector $(p_{1},p_{2},\ldots,p_{q})$ explicitly with the following algorithm:

We need to show two things. First, for any $I\subsetneq[q],$ it must be the case that $\sum_{j\in I}p_{j}\leq g(\bigcup_{j\in I}S_{j}).$ Second, the fact that $\sum_{j\in[q]}p_{j}\geq g(S)/\mathcal{H}_{q-1}.$ Technically, we also need to show that the inequality $\sum_{j\in[q]}p_{j}\leq g(S)$ holds. However, if this condition is violated, we can reduce prices until $\sum_{j\in[q]}p_{j}\leq g(S)$ without violating any other conditions.

First, take some $I\subsetneq[q].$ Consider the iteration of the algorithm in which the $\ell^{\prime}$ th price indexed by an element in $I$ is determined. Since the algorithm could have chosen $I$ in that iteration, it must be the case that

$$ \frac{g(\bigcup_{i\in A}S_{i})}{|A\backslash C|}\leq\frac{g(\bigcup_{i\in I}S_{i})}{|I\backslash C|}\leq\frac{g(\bigcup_{i\in I}S_{i})}{|I|-\ell+1}. $$

Therefore,

$$ \sum_{i\in I}p_{i}\leq\sum_{\ell=1}^{|I|}\frac{g(\bigcup_{i\in I}S_{i})}{\mathcal{H}_{q-1}(|I|-\ell+1)}\leq\frac{g(\bigcup_{i\in I}S_{i})}{\mathcal{H}_{q-1}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{|I|}\frac{1}{\ell}\leq g(\bigcup_{i\in I}S_{i}), $$

as desired (we used the fact that $|I|\leq q-1$ ). Now, we will analyze $\sum_{i\in[q]}p_{i}.$ Let the index sets chosen by the algorithm be $A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{t}.$ Then,

$$ \sum_{i\in[q]}p_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{t}\sum_{i\in A_{j}}p_{j}=\sum_{j=1}^{t}|A_{j}|\times\frac{g(\bigcup_{i\in A_{j}}S_{i})}{\mathcal{H}_{q-1}\times|A_{j}|}=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{t}g(\bigcup_{i\in A_{j}}S_{i})}{\mathcal{H}_{q-1}}\geq\frac{g(S)}{\mathcal{H}_{q-1}}, $$

where we used subadditivity in the last equality. ∎

A simple modification of [BR11, Appendix C] shows that Proposition G.0.1 is tight up to a constant multiplicative factor.

#### Proposition G.0.2.

For any $2<q\leq m,$ the class of subadditive valuations over $[m]$ is not $\gamma$ -close to $\mathcal{Q}(q,[m])$ for any $\gamma>\frac{2}{\log_{2}\frac{q}{2}}.$

#### Proof.

Let $q^{\prime}$ be the largest integer such that $q^{\prime}\leq q$ and $q^{\prime}=2^{a}-1$ for some natural number $a.$ Note that $q^{\prime}\geq\frac{q}{2}.$ Then, one can construct as in [BR11, Appendix C] a subadditive valuation $g$ over $[q^{\prime}]$ that is not $\gamma$ -close to being XOS for any $\gamma>\frac{2}{\log_{2}\frac{q}{2}}$ as follows.

Construction in [BR11, Appendix C]: Identify $[q^{\prime}]$ with the set $\mathcal{V}$ of $2^{a}-1$ non-zero vectors over the finite vector space $F_{2}^{a}.$ For each $v\in\mathcal{V},$ set $S_{v}=\{u\in\mathcal{V}\;:v\cdot u\equiv 1\pmod{2}\}.$ Define $g$ as the set-cover function over $\mathcal{V}.$ On the one hand, we can observe that $g(\mathcal{V})\geq a.$ Indeed, for any $r<a$ vectors $v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{r},$ we can find some $u$ such that $v_{i}\cdot u=0\pmod{2}$ holds for all $i\in[r]$ simply because the matrix $(v_{1}\;v_{2}\;\cdots\;v_{r})^{T}$ is not of full rank. On the other hand, note that for each $v,$ the set $S_{v}$ contains $2^{a-1}$ elements and each $u\in\mathcal{V}$ belongs to $2^{a-1}$ sets of the form $S_{v}.$ Since $g(S_{v})=1,$ the fractional cover $\alpha$ assigning weight $\frac{1}{2^{a-1}}$ to each set $S_{v}$ satisfies

$$ \sum_{I\subseteq\mathcal{V}}\alpha(I)g(I)=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\alpha(S_{v})g(S_{v})=(2^{a}-1)\times\frac{1}{2^{a-1}}\leq 2, $$

which shows that $g$ is not $\gamma$ -close to being XOS for $\gamma>\frac{2}{a}\geq\frac{2}{\log_{2}\frac{q}{2}}.$

Now, we go back to the problem statement. Clearly, $q^{\prime}\leq q\leq m.$ First, we extend $g$ to a subadditive valuation $g^{\prime}$ on $[m]$ by setting $g^{\prime}(S):=g(S\cap[q^{\prime}])$ for any $S\subseteq[m].$ It trivially follows that $g^{\prime}$ is not $\gamma$ -close to any $q^{\prime}$ -partitioning valuation for any $\gamma>\frac{2}{\log_{2}\frac{q}{2}}^{\prime}.$ As $q^{\prime}\leq q,$ meaning that any $q$ -partitioning valuation is also $q^{\prime}$ -partitioning, the result follows. ∎
